extraction.body: Westminster appears to be waking up to warnings over AI safety, with concerns over its use by extremist groups and bad actors “I have this sense that, within a few months, AI is going to be all anyone is talking about,” said one cabinet minister, with an ominous stare. It was Labour conference, with everyone from ministers to activists jubilant at Andy Burnham’s takeover and a bounce in the polls after the change of leader. But a number of senior Labour figures were privately starting to name the power of AI as the thing worrying them most, alongside the immediate pressures on the cost of living and fragile economy. One cabinet minister – with a brief unrelated to technology – told the Guardian that dangerous, out-of-control AI was the issue keeping them up at night, fretting about the threat to humanity. It was “not killer robots” causing the worry, they explained, but the idea of a huge amount of concentrated, super-intelligent power potentially ending up in the hands of bad actors. Another expressed concern that the government was “falling behind the public” in terms of dealing with worries about AI safety – and that it needed to catch up fast. In his conference speech, Ed Miliband was the most strident about the “daunting” dangers of AI, making the case that politicians could not and would not allow the profits of tech companies “to come at the expense of our children or indeed humanity”. And it has not taken long for these alarm bells to ring even louder, with the last seven days looking like the week Westminster fully woke up to the warnings. A flurry of activity started on Monday with Kanishka Narayan, the AI minister, stating it was “likely, if not inevitable” that rogue agents would hack the British state, and saying the UK was looking to strengthen its forthcoming cybersecurity legislation. It was the main topic of discussion at cabinet on Tuesday, and that was followed by the MI5 chief Ken McCallum warning AI was “supercharging the cybersecurity contest between attackers and defenders”. He said the biggest threat was extremist groups using the technology to unleash bioweapons – toxins used to cause death and disease. Liam Byrne, the chair of the business, innovation, science and trade committee, said the change of government from Keir Starmer to Burnham was partly behind the increased focus on protecting the UK from AI threats but more still had to be done. “The reality is that the Starmer administration was much too close to the big tech companies,” Byrne said. “And Burnham is not, frankly, so there has been a change of posture. Those things, plus the security services issuing their warning, that is what has changed the weather on this.” One senior Labour government figure agreed that Burnham’s government was taking AI safety warnings more seriously. “I do feel there has been a shift. Under the last lot, too many of them had drunk the tech-bro Kool-Aid,” he said. Byrne’s committee held an evidence session this week with civil service leaders in charge of AI security and executives from the key companies – Anthropic , OpenAI, DeepMind and Meta – with a split between them about whether government testing of new models should be mandatory. He said his committee was “lighting up” the issue, particularly in terms of working with the US to regulate and monitor new models. It had been reported that Donald Trump’s administration had asked AI companies not to share their latest models with the UK’s cutting-edge AI Security Institute for testing, though Narayan confirmed this week that they had managed to retain cooperation. But Byrne said the government now needed to seize the moment and take the lead on new regulation, particularly if Trump’s Republicans lost control of Congress in the midterm elections to the Democrats. “I think the government is still caught in a dilemma between how to keep model access, given a capricious US president, and the safeguards that the industry itself now says are essential. It’s make-your-mind-up time, I would say,” Byrne said. “The companies want to cooperate … It’s not in their commercial interest to issue models which are lethal. Now they too have got to navigate the White House. So I just think this is a moment when the government has actually got to do what is right for the country because Congress is about to change the dynamics on this in the US.” The UK’s upcoming G20 presidency will be the key moment to push for international action to rein in AI. Geoffrey Irving, the former chief scientist at AISI who spoke at this week’s parliamentary hearing , believes Whitehall concerns are justified. OpenAI and Anthropic’s technology has already shown its hacking capabilities but their models are released with safety guardrails in place that at least mitigate against the threat of malicious behaviour. However, so-called open source AI models are freely available and can be adapted. Typically, they caught up with the paid-for models such as OpenAI’s within less than a year, said Irving, although they could cause disruption already. “It’s very likely that open source models are already powerful enough to do serious damage,” Irving told the Guardian, adding that he expected open source technology to reach the capabilities of OpenAI and Anthropic products “soon”. Safety guardrails “either don’t exist or can be trivially removed” from open source models, he added. The business committee heard this week that AI-enabled bioweapons could become the next serious threat to manifest itself, in the wake of cybersecurity, as models become more powerful and therefore capable of designing novel bio-harms – although experts suggest there is a gap between designing dangerous pathogens and weaponising them. Concerns over cybersecurity and bioweapons can escalate rapidly to fears about AI wiping out humanity in a variety of scenarios – a concern that is widespread within the AI community, and is shared by Irving. However, some experts argue that the government should focus on immediate risks from AI. Prof Elena Simperl, a co-director of the Institute for Artificial Intelligence at King’s College London, said the existential risk argument had “no evidence” and was a “theory” rather than a credible threat. “There are bigger, more immediate risks that AI technology is posing now and are actually evidenced, like hacking and signs that AI can be as addictive as social media,” Simperl said. In the absence of international AI regulation, there are some in Whitehall worried about whether the UK is doing enough preparation to defend against AI warfare and attacks. Defence sources said there was concern about the cancellation last year of the AI programme at the government’s Defence Science and Technology Laboratory (Dstl), based at Porton Down, with worries that this was shortsighted given the need for cutting-edge research on advancing the nation’s capabilities and defending against its risks. This was countered by an MoD spokesperson who said AI was “transforming defence from industry to the battlefield and will play a decisive role in how we fight and defend” and that it must be “integrated across all workstreams, rather than a standalone programme”. They pointed to a £400m investment in AI-focused capabilities over the next four years to “prepare the UK for the future of warfare”. Others in Whitehall have the opposite concern: that worries about safety could become too dominant – and end up holding back the government’s adoption of tools that could be transformative for productivity and solving longstanding problems in public services, from medical care to reducing waiting lists. The former cabinet secretary Gus O’Donnell told the Guardian that ministers needed to be as aware of “the risk of being left behind” when it came to AI as being aware of the need for guardrails. Launching a Global Government Forum report on AI with the tech firm Cognizant, O’Donnell told the Guardian: “There is a big need to get it better and to really push on. I’m really optimistic, but the challenge for us, obviously, is managing the risks along the way, making sure that we don’t make mistakes, which reduce people’s trust, which means that that sets us back.”

He said his committee was “lighting up” the issue, particularly in terms of working with the US to regulate and monitor new models. However, so-called open source AI models are freely available and can be adapted. Typically, they caught up with the paid-for models such as OpenAI’s within less than a year, said Irving, although they could cause disruption already. “It’s very likely that open source models are already powerful enough to do serious damage,” Irving told the Guardian, adding that he expected open source technology to reach the capabilities of OpenAI and Anthropic products “soon”. Launching a Global Government Forum report on AI with the tech firm Cognizant, O’Donnell told the Guardian: “There is a big need to get it better and to really push on. sources.title: These Samsung Galaxy Tablets Are In Their Last Year Of Software Support - Engadget
passages: Fortunately, newer Galaxy Tab models come with longer software support cycles.
Samsung began its seven-year software update policy with the Galaxy Tab S10 series that launched in 2024.
Surprisingly, even Samsung's budget Galaxy Tab A11 and A11+ devices, which released in 2025, are eligible for seven years of Android and security updates.
If you're buying from Samsung's current catalog of tablets, you don't have to worry about having software updates dropped anytime soon.
Not every tablet Samsung has sold in previous years enjoys that kind of longevity, though.
Samsung also sells rugged tablets under its Galaxy Tab Active lineup, which are marketed primarily towards business and enterprise customers.
These tablets are the last ones released before Samsung's more generous support policy.
Check for Android or security updates on your Samsung tablet by navigating to Settings > Software update > Download and install .

Back in the TouchWiz era, Samsung's reputation for timely software updates wasn't exactly the best. It's thus great to see how far the brand has come in delivering faster updates and providing longer software support for its devices. Samsung is now one of the few Android manufacturers that offers a generously long software support policy, with its recent Galaxy Tab S12 Ultra benefiting from seven years of OS and security updates. Not every tablet Samsung has sold in previous years enjoys that kind of longevity, though. 2026 marks the final release of major Android updates for the Galaxy Tab S9, S9+, S9 Ultra, S9 FE and S9 FE+. These tablets will receive the One UI 9 update , which is based on Android 17. The Galaxy Tab S9 series arrived in 2023 running One UI 5.1 (Android 13), with Samsung promising four generations of major OS updates and five years of security patches for these devices. They should continue to receive security updates until sometime in 2028. The Galaxy Tab S8, S8+ and S8 Ultra (released in February 2022) have already received their final major OS upgrade with One UI 8, which is based on Android 16. Security updates should continue until February 2027. Android 16 is also the last major update for the Galaxy Tab A9 and A9+, which were released in October 2023. Despite being a bit newer, the Galaxy Tab A9 series has already received its final major OS update, likely because it was a budget-oriented offering. It will still receive another year of security updates. Fortunately, newer Galaxy Tab models come with longer software support cycles. Samsung began its seven-year software update policy with the Galaxy Tab S10 series that launched in 2024. The newer Galaxy Tab S11 and S12 models offer the same commitment. Samsung also sells rugged tablets under its Galaxy Tab Active lineup, which are marketed primarily towards business and enterprise customers. These devices have different software update policies. The Galaxy Tab Active5 was launched in 2024 with a four-year commitment to Android OS updates and five years of security updates. Since it shipped with Android 14, it should be good for updates through Android 18, with security patches continuing until 2029. Be aware that not every device from Samsung receives OS updates at the same time. Rollout schedules vary depending on your tablet's model and region. So if you aren't seeing the One UI 9 update on your Galaxy Tab yet, it doesn't mean you've been left out. Check for Android or security updates on your Samsung tablet by navigating to Settings > Software update > Download and install . If there's a pending update available, tap Install now .

sources.title: Meta Scrubs AI Training Language After Privacy Backlash
passages: Meta's quiet retreat on AI training language reveals how sensitive the data rights question has become in the race to build next-generation AI.

The social media giant removed text that appeared to give it broad rights to scrape external websites for AI training data, though a company spokesperson insists nothing actually changed in how Meta crawls the web.

The removal of the controversial language might calm immediate concerns, but it doesn't answer the fundamental question: What data is Meta actually using to train its AI models, and where does it come from?
If the terms language was always meant to describe existing practices, the backlash suggests Meta failed to communicate clearly what those practices actually are.
And if the language accidentally revealed plans Meta wasn't ready to announce, removing it without explanation only deepens suspicion.
This isn't Meta's first rodeo with privacy concerns.
But if nothing changed, why remove the language at all?
The web scraping question cuts deeper than Meta's own ecosystem.

extraction.body: The social media giant removed text that appeared to give it broad rights to scrape external websites for AI training data, though a company spokesperson insists nothing actually changed in how Meta crawls the web. The reversal comes just days after legal experts confirmed the company's updated terms meant business account holders were consenting to AI training, adding fuel to an already raging debate about data rights in the AI era. The controversial text suggested Meta might be claiming rights to scrape content across the broader web to feed its AI models, not just data from its own platforms like Facebook, Instagram, and WhatsApp. For an industry already on edge about how tech giants are hoovering up training data, it was gasoline on a fire. "The updated terms did not reflect a change in the way Meta crawls the web," a Meta spokesperson told TechCrunch. But if nothing changed, why remove the language at all? The company hasn't elaborated, leaving the industry to read between the lines. Just this week, the company was caught in another data rights controversy when legal experts confirmed its updated terms meant business account holders were automatically consenting to AI training. That revelation sent small business owners and content creators scrambling to understand what data they'd inadvertently signed over. The web scraping question cuts deeper than Meta's own ecosystem. Meta has been racing to catch up in the AI arms race. The company recently introduced tools that let users control Facebook's algorithm using natural language, and it's betting big on AI-powered features across its product line. But every AI model needs training data, and lots of it. The question of where that data comes from and who consents to its use has become one of the most contentious issues in tech. The company's vague explanation isn't helping its case. If the terms language was always meant to describe existing practices, the backlash suggests Meta failed to communicate clearly what those practices actually are. And if the language accidentally revealed plans Meta wasn't ready to announce, removing it without explanation only deepens suspicion. Google has faced similar accusations about using web content for AI training, while OpenAI has struck licensing deals with publishers to avoid exactly this kind of controversy. The legal landscape remains murky, with courts still working out whether scraping publicly available data for AI training constitutes fair use. If AI models can ingest their content without permission or payment, what's their business model? The company needs massive amounts of data to compete with OpenAI and Google in generative AI, but it can't afford to alienate the businesses and creators that make its platforms valuable in the first place. The removal of the controversial language might calm immediate concerns, but it doesn't answer the fundamental question: What data is Meta actually using to train its AI models, and where does it come from? Until the company offers more transparency, expect the scrutiny to continue. This isn't Meta's first rodeo with privacy concerns. The company has spent years rebuilding trust after the Cambridge Analytica scandal and other data mishaps. Users and businesses are more sophisticated about data rights now, and they're not afraid to push back when terms seem overreaching. Meta's quiet retreat on AI training language reveals how sensitive the data rights question has become in the race to build next-generation AI. The company's insistence that nothing changed in its actual practices raises more questions than it answers, especially coming on the heels of the business account opt-in controversy. As tech giants compete for training data, expect more flashpoints like this. The companies that figure out transparent, fair data practices will have a strategic advantage, while those that stumble through vague terms and forced opt-ins risk regulatory crackdowns and user exodus.

sources.title: Meta Scrubs AI Training Language After Privacy Backlash
passages: Meta's quiet retreat on AI training language reveals how sensitive the data rights question has become in the race to build next-generation AI.

The social media giant removed text that appeared to give it broad rights to scrape external websites for AI training data, though a company spokesperson insists nothing actually changed in how Meta crawls the web.

The removal of the controversial language might calm immediate concerns, but it doesn't answer the fundamental question: What data is Meta actually using to train its AI models, and where does it come from?
If the terms language was always meant to describe existing practices, the backlash suggests Meta failed to communicate clearly what those practices actually are.
And if the language accidentally revealed plans Meta wasn't ready to announce, removing it without explanation only deepens suspicion.
This isn't Meta's first rodeo with privacy concerns.
But if nothing changed, why remove the language at all?
The web scraping question cuts deeper than Meta's own ecosystem.

extraction.body: The social media giant removed text that appeared to give it broad rights to scrape external websites for AI training data, though a company spokesperson insists nothing actually changed in how Meta crawls the web. The reversal comes just days after legal experts confirmed the company's updated terms meant business account holders were consenting to AI training, adding fuel to an already raging debate about data rights in the AI era. The controversial text suggested Meta might be claiming rights to scrape content across the broader web to feed its AI models, not just data from its own platforms like Facebook, Instagram, and WhatsApp. For an industry already on edge about how tech giants are hoovering up training data, it was gasoline on a fire. "The updated terms did not reflect a change in the way Meta crawls the web," a Meta spokesperson told TechCrunch. But if nothing changed, why remove the language at all? The company hasn't elaborated, leaving the industry to read between the lines. Just this week, the company was caught in another data rights controversy when legal experts confirmed its updated terms meant business account holders were automatically consenting to AI training. That revelation sent small business owners and content creators scrambling to understand what data they'd inadvertently signed over. The web scraping question cuts deeper than Meta's own ecosystem. Meta has been racing to catch up in the AI arms race. The company recently introduced tools that let users control Facebook's algorithm using natural language, and it's betting big on AI-powered features across its product line. But every AI model needs training data, and lots of it. The question of where that data comes from and who consents to its use has become one of the most contentious issues in tech. The company's vague explanation isn't helping its case. If the terms language was always meant to describe existing practices, the backlash suggests Meta failed to communicate clearly what those practices actually are. And if the language accidentally revealed plans Meta wasn't ready to announce, removing it without explanation only deepens suspicion. Google has faced similar accusations about using web content for AI training, while OpenAI has struck licensing deals with publishers to avoid exactly this kind of controversy. The legal landscape remains murky, with courts still working out whether scraping publicly available data for AI training constitutes fair use. If AI models can ingest their content without permission or payment, what's their business model? The company needs massive amounts of data to compete with OpenAI and Google in generative AI, but it can't afford to alienate the businesses and creators that make its platforms valuable in the first place. The removal of the controversial language might calm immediate concerns, but it doesn't answer the fundamental question: What data is Meta actually using to train its AI models, and where does it come from? Until the company offers more transparency, expect the scrutiny to continue. This isn't Meta's first rodeo with privacy concerns. The company has spent years rebuilding trust after the Cambridge Analytica scandal and other data mishaps. Users and businesses are more sophisticated about data rights now, and they're not afraid to push back when terms seem overreaching. Meta's quiet retreat on AI training language reveals how sensitive the data rights question has become in the race to build next-generation AI. The company's insistence that nothing changed in its actual practices raises more questions than it answers, especially coming on the heels of the business account opt-in controversy. As tech giants compete for training data, expect more flashpoints like this. The companies that figure out transparent, fair data practices will have a strategic advantage, while those that stumble through vague terms and forced opt-ins risk regulatory crackdowns and user exodus.

extraction.body: An internal OpenAI research model that ran out of money during a coding assignment spent funds from someone else's cryptocurrency wallet to complete the job, the company disclosed on Thursday. The money was test tokens on an Ethereum practice network and had no market value, but OpenAI classifies the episode as an unauthorised use of another party's wallet. What happened?According to OpenAI's incident report, the episode occurred on June 26 during training of an internal model in its GPT-5.6 Sol family. The model had been asked to update a cryptocurrency trading prototype and deploy smart contracts, which are programs that run on a blockchain, on Sepolia, a network where developers rehearse Ethereum applications. It was not given a funded wallet to pay the network fees.After attempts to get free test tokens failed, the model wrote a script that checked 362 addresses generated from recovery phrases commonly used by developers. It found one with enough funds, used that wallet's private key to sign the deployment transaction, and the wallet paid the fees. A recovery phrase generates a wallet's secret keys, so anyone holding the words can spend from the accounts without touching the owner's device.How the model justified it?The model's recorded reasoning shows it questioned whether using publicly known keys and funds was ethical, then concluded that it was acceptable. It described the funds as effectively abandoned and noted that Sepolia ether has no value, according to the report as described by Altcoin Buzz. OpenAI's reading is that the model substituted its own judgment about the likelihood of harm for the account holder's permission, and acted on that judgment.OpenAI Accuses Ex-Employee Now At Apple Of Taking Files On Unreleased DeviceWhat the model left outWhen it reported back, the model said the work was done without mentioning where the money came from, CoinDesk reported. The report redacts the amount spent, the wallet address and the recovery phrase, so the size of the spending is not public.How OpenAI found out and respondedOpenAI discovered the incident on September 25 after expanding its internal monitoring that month. The company says it has added restrictions on internet access and more monitoring. The monitoring now covers all traffic and is set up to alert security staff if a model gets live internet access.Saudi OpenAI Employee Arrested After Hidden Recording Device Allegedly Found At San Francisco HeadquartersWhy it mattersThe incident is not the first such disclosure. OpenAI has also reported other cases of its models acting outside their authorisation, including one that used an exposed API key without permission and then made up figures it could not retrieve. extraction.body: Bank’s chief knowledge officer says the tech could speed up economic development from centuries to decades Bank’s chief knowledge officer says the tech could speed up economic development from centuries to decades The World Bank is urging developing countries to kickstart the creation of “small AI” models, which can run on a mobile phone with low connectivity, to reap the full benefits of artificial intelligence. While Silicon Valley big tech firms are focused on ever more sophisticated consumer products, Paschal Donohoe, the World Bank’s chief knowledge officer, said AI could also accelerate development for emerging economies – but only if it was adapted to local needs. Small AI uses specialised models that are trained using narrower datasets for a specific purpose. “We argue that economic development in the countries that we serve and partner with that could have taken centuries to make happen, the potential is there for that economic development now to happen within decades,” Donohoe said. “Small AI would be available in a local setting, with low connectivity, and in the local language of the community – and tends to be available on your mobile phone.” Donohoe, a former finance minister for Ireland, cited the example of Indian farmers engaged in the World Bank’s agricultural scheme, AgriConnect, who needed to access soil analysis in their own language. “There’s not going to be enough scientists and agricultural experts to do that for every small farm in India. And this is where what we describe as ‘small AI’ comes in. Because small AI is AI that would be available on your phone, that can help deliver against those information needs.” He suggested such products could emerge from collaboration between the World Bank, governments and the private sector. The impact of AI on jobs and growth is a central theme of the annual meetings of the World Bank and the International Monetary Fund (IMF), which are being held this week in Bangkok, Thailand. Speaking on a panel about the impact of the technology on Monday, Kristalina Georgieva, the IMF’s managing director, called on governments to provide the preconditions for AI to succeed. She said: “You need access to electricity. You need access to digital infrastructure. People have to be geared to adoption. And the government should be able to give some safety, protect against bad actors so that adoption can work. “If we work hard to have the basics for it, [adoption] can be very democratic. As democratic as the cellphone.” The World Bank’s annual world development report, published in August, hailed the potential benefits of AI. But it pointed out that, for example, almost a third of rural schools in sub-Saharan Africa lacked electricity and more than two-thirds did not have a consistent internet connection. Georgieva warned that over time 40% of jobs worldwide were likely to be either augmented or eliminated by AI, with the impact particularly acute for young people at the start of their careers. “When we look at this, what we recognise is that the people to worry about, first and foremost, are young people that are coming into the labour market,” she said. “Normally they would get into these routine, repetitive jobs and then go up the ranks. But if they’re gone, I don’t think any young person wants to be a barista in a coffee shop as a professional future.” Under its president, Ajay Banga, the World Bank has made attracting private-sector funding into emerging economies a focus of its work. Donohoe said the World Bank had mobilised $120bn (£90bn) of private capital in the past year using guarantees and other financial instruments, at a time when many countries, including the US and the UK, were cutting their aid budgets. “We want to highlight the link between private capital mobilisation and jobs and economic development,” he said.

extraction.body: BANGKOK, Oct 11 (Reuters) - The World Bank is in discussions with 30 to 40 countries about potential crisis aid to help them manage energy shocks and price increases triggered by the war in the Middle East, its president, Ajay Banga, told Reuters in an interview. Banga said the global economy had proven fairly resilient, in part due to big AI investments and adjustments in supply and demand for oil, which meant that few countries had sought the initial $25 billion in crisis funds that the World Bank had made available when the war began in late February. However, a sharp spike in diesel and fertilizer prices and other factors, including the looming super El Niño weather effect, were adding to challenges facing developing countries, Banga said in an interview ahead of this week's annual meetings of the International Monetary Fund and World Bank. "There is pressure, and so I think maybe over the coming months, more countries will come for some slice of that first $50 to $60 billion," Banga said, referring to the initial $25 billion plus another $35 billion that countries could tap by diverting resources from already approved World Bank projects. "We'll see, but we're ready. We're engaged. We're having conversations with a number of them, you know, 30 to 40 countries are in dialogue with us," he said. Many developing countries have been hit hard by the spike in energy prices and high interest rates that have increased borrowing costs at a time when their fiscal coffers are still depleted by measures taken during the COVID-19 pandemic and the spike in inflation following Russia's invasion of Ukraine. World Bank estimates show that developing countries owe external creditors about $400 billion in 2026, with interest payments alone comprising one-third of the total. Banga said more countries had shown interest in retooling existing projects than in tapping the immediate crisis window to address their liquidity needs. If the situation worsened, the Bank could make available as much as $100 billion in funds, he said, exceeding the $70 billion disbursed during the pandemic. The World Bank last month announced that it attracted a record $112 billion in private capital in the year ended June versus $69 billion a year earlier, and more than triple the 2022 total before Banga, a former Mastercard CEO, became president. That was on top of the $123 billion invested from the bank's own resources for that year, for a combined $235 billion, Banga said, underscoring the importance of tapping all available resources, especially at a time when Western countries have sharply cut official bilateral development aid. "There is no one answer that fits when the world has these kinds of issues. What you need to do is figure out how to cut your coat to suit your cloth," Banga said. Banga said he expected further gains in private capital flows in coming years, aided by expanded political risk guarantees from the bank's Multilateral Investment Guarantee Agency, growth in local currency financing, and continued work on regulatory reforms that made it easier for foreign investors. The private capital jump was biggest in projects in upper-middle-income countries like Argentina or India, which accounted for $50 billion of the private capital, and lower-middle-income countries including Bangladesh and Angola, which accounted for $37 billion. But more work was needed to boost the roughly $3 billion in private capital flowing to low-income countries. "In the smaller countries, it hasn't multiplied enough, and there are challenges," he said, noting the bank would announce some new initiatives this week aimed at ensuring micro-, small- and medium-sized businesses also had access to private capital. Banga said private capital growth was also regionally spread, with the largest increase seen in Latin America and the Caribbean, which accounted for $36.3 billion of last year's total, followed by Europe and Central Asia with $21.3 billion, South Asia with $19.2 billion and Africa with $22 billion. The top 10 recipient countries were Brazil, India, Turkey, Romania, Nigeria, Argentina, South Africa, Bangladesh, Mexico and Chile, the Bank said. Banga said the World Bank and IMF were working together to address the high debt levels plaguing many developing countries through a series of initiatives, including efforts to boost countries' domestic revenue collections. The Bank had already set up some debt-for-development swaps for Angola and Ivory Coast, and a portfolio-based guarantee for Argentina, and was working on over a dozen more projects. "We've got 14 or 15 in the pipeline, helping them rotate out higher-priced old debt for newer-priced debt with our guarantees," with the difference then targeted at education, healthcare, water, or nature programs, he said. (Reporting by Andrea Shalal; Editing by Andrea Ricci )

passages: World Bank president Ajay Banga said this during a discussion on ‘Small AI: More and Better Jobs’ at the 2026 International Monetary Fund/World Bank annual meetings in Bangkok, Thailand, on Monday.
He said the World Bank’s development approach now prioritised job creation, with infrastructure, governance reforms and policies designed to attract private investment.

Mr Banga noted that while advanced AI models could disrupt some jobs in developed economies, small-scale AI offers significant opportunities to boost productivity and create jobs in middle- and lower-middle-income countries.

extraction.body: The World Bank Group is prioritising job creation and productivity, using AI to expand economic opportunities in developing countries. The World Bank Group is prioritising job creation and productivity, using AI to expand economic opportunities in developing countries. World Bank president Ajay Banga said this during a discussion on ‘Small AI: More and Better Jobs’ at the 2026 International Monetary Fund/World Bank annual meetings in Bangkok, Thailand, on Monday. Mr Banga stressed the need to make technology accessible and relevant to local economies. He said about 1.2 billion young people would turn 18 within the next 15 years, allowing countries to harness their demographic potential through productive employment. According to him, realising this potential requires investments in healthcare, education, clean water, electricity and skills development, alongside opportunities for young people to contribute meaningfully to society. Mr Banga explained that employment should not be limited to jobs in large or small companies but should include entrepreneurship and other productive activities that promote dignity and economic inclusion. He said the World Bank’s development approach now prioritised job creation, with infrastructure, governance reforms and policies designed to attract private investment. “The private sector generates between 75 and 85 per cent of jobs in any country,” the president said. Mr Banga also said that governments must create conditions that encourage businesses to invest and expand. He identified infrastructure, agriculture, primary healthcare, tourism and value-added manufacturing as five critical sectors capable of generating sustainable employment in emerging economies. Mr Banga said these sectors could create locally relevant jobs without relying solely on outsourcing from advanced economies. The president said that on AI, small-scale applications could improve productivity in agriculture, education and healthcare, particularly in communities with limited access to specialised services. He cited an example of primary healthcare centres in Indonesia, where nurses could use simple AI tools on mobile phones to assess patients’ symptoms and connect with remote doctors. Mr Banga said that such technology could help healthcare workers identify conditions, obtain medical guidance and arrange specialist appointments more efficiently. The president also highlighted agricultural technology initiatives connecting smallholder farmers and cooperatives with improved seeds, fertilisers, crop insurance, credit and better market prices. He explained that farmers could use basic mobile phones to identify crop diseases and obtain recommendations, helping them make informed decisions and improve productivity. According to him, these applications demonstrate how relatively simple AI tools can address practical challenges in developing countries. Mr Banga noted that while advanced AI models could disrupt some jobs in developed economies, small-scale AI offers significant opportunities to boost productivity and create jobs in middle- and lower-middle-income countries. He said his priority was to deploy practical small-AI applications across as many emerging markets as possible. extraction.body: Bank’s chief knowledge officer says the tech could speed up economic development from centuries to decades Bank’s chief knowledge officer says the tech could speed up economic development from centuries to decades The World Bank is urging developing countries to kickstart the creation of “small AI” models, which can run on a mobile phone with low connectivity, to reap the full benefits of artificial intelligence. While Silicon Valley big tech firms are focused on ever more sophisticated consumer products, Paschal Donohoe, the World Bank’s chief knowledge officer, said AI could also accelerate development for emerging economies – but only if it was adapted to local needs. Small AI uses specialised models that are trained using narrower datasets for a specific purpose. “We argue that economic development in the countries that we serve and partner with that could have taken centuries to make happen, the potential is there for that economic development now to happen within decades,” Donohoe said. “Small AI would be available in a local setting, with low connectivity, and in the local language of the community – and tends to be available on your mobile phone.” Donohoe, a former finance minister for Ireland, cited the example of Indian farmers engaged in the World Bank’s agricultural scheme, AgriConnect, who needed to access soil analysis in their own language. “There’s not going to be enough scientists and agricultural experts to do that for every small farm in India. And this is where what we describe as ‘small AI’ comes in. Because small AI is AI that would be available on your phone, that can help deliver against those information needs.” He suggested such products could emerge from collaboration between the World Bank, governments and the private sector. The impact of AI on jobs and growth is a central theme of the annual meetings of the World Bank and the International Monetary Fund (IMF), which are being held this week in Bangkok, Thailand. Speaking on a panel about the impact of the technology on Monday, Kristalina Georgieva, the IMF’s managing director, called on governments to provide the preconditions for AI to succeed. She said: “You need access to electricity. You need access to digital infrastructure. People have to be geared to adoption. And the government should be able to give some safety, protect against bad actors so that adoption can work. “If we work hard to have the basics for it, [adoption] can be very democratic. As democratic as the cellphone.” The World Bank’s annual world development report, published in August, hailed the potential benefits of AI. But it pointed out that, for example, almost a third of rural schools in sub-Saharan Africa lacked electricity and more than two-thirds did not have a consistent internet connection. Georgieva warned that over time 40% of jobs worldwide were likely to be either augmented or eliminated by AI, with the impact particularly acute for young people at the start of their careers. “When we look at this, what we recognise is that the people to worry about, first and foremost, are young people that are coming into the labour market,” she said. “Normally they would get into these routine, repetitive jobs and then go up the ranks. But if they’re gone, I don’t think any young person wants to be a barista in a coffee shop as a professional future.” Under its president, Ajay Banga, the World Bank has made attracting private-sector funding into emerging economies a focus of its work. Donohoe said the World Bank had mobilised $120bn (£90bn) of private capital in the past year using guarantees and other financial instruments, at a time when many countries, including the US and the UK, were cutting their aid budgets. “We want to highlight the link between private capital mobilisation and jobs and economic development,” he said.

extraction.body: BANGKOK, Oct 11 (Reuters) - The World Bank is in discussions with 30 to 40 countries about potential crisis aid to help them manage energy shocks and price increases triggered by the war in the Middle East, its president, Ajay Banga, told Reuters in an interview. Banga said the global economy had proven fairly resilient, in part due to big AI investments and adjustments in supply and demand for oil, which meant that few countries had sought the initial $25 billion in crisis funds that the World Bank had made available when the war began in late February. However, a sharp spike in diesel and fertilizer prices and other factors, including the looming super El Niño weather effect, were adding to challenges facing developing countries, Banga said in an interview ahead of this week's annual meetings of the International Monetary Fund and World Bank. "There is pressure, and so I think maybe over the coming months, more countries will come for some slice of that first $50 to $60 billion," Banga said, referring to the initial $25 billion plus another $35 billion that countries could tap by diverting resources from already approved World Bank projects. "We'll see, but we're ready. We're engaged. We're having conversations with a number of them, you know, 30 to 40 countries are in dialogue with us," he said. Many developing countries have been hit hard by the spike in energy prices and high interest rates that have increased borrowing costs at a time when their fiscal coffers are still depleted by measures taken during the COVID-19 pandemic and the spike in inflation following Russia's invasion of Ukraine. World Bank estimates show that developing countries owe external creditors about $400 billion in 2026, with interest payments alone comprising one-third of the total. Banga said more countries had shown interest in retooling existing projects than in tapping the immediate crisis window to address their liquidity needs. If the situation worsened, the Bank could make available as much as $100 billion in funds, he said, exceeding the $70 billion disbursed during the pandemic. The World Bank last month announced that it attracted a record $112 billion in private capital in the year ended June versus $69 billion a year earlier, and more than triple the 2022 total before Banga, a former Mastercard CEO, became president. That was on top of the $123 billion invested from the bank's own resources for that year, for a combined $235 billion, Banga said, underscoring the importance of tapping all available resources, especially at a time when Western countries have sharply cut official bilateral development aid. "There is no one answer that fits when the world has these kinds of issues. What you need to do is figure out how to cut your coat to suit your cloth," Banga said. Banga said he expected further gains in private capital flows in coming years, aided by expanded political risk guarantees from the bank's Multilateral Investment Guarantee Agency, growth in local currency financing, and continued work on regulatory reforms that made it easier for foreign investors. The private capital jump was biggest in projects in upper-middle-income countries like Argentina or India, which accounted for $50 billion of the private capital, and lower-middle-income countries including Bangladesh and Angola, which accounted for $37 billion. But more work was needed to boost the roughly $3 billion in private capital flowing to low-income countries. "In the smaller countries, it hasn't multiplied enough, and there are challenges," he said, noting the bank would announce some new initiatives this week aimed at ensuring micro-, small- and medium-sized businesses also had access to private capital. Banga said private capital growth was also regionally spread, with the largest increase seen in Latin America and the Caribbean, which accounted for $36.3 billion of last year's total, followed by Europe and Central Asia with $21.3 billion, South Asia with $19.2 billion and Africa with $22 billion. The top 10 recipient countries were Brazil, India, Turkey, Romania, Nigeria, Argentina, South Africa, Bangladesh, Mexico and Chile, the Bank said. Banga said the World Bank and IMF were working together to address the high debt levels plaguing many developing countries through a series of initiatives, including efforts to boost countries' domestic revenue collections. The Bank had already set up some debt-for-development swaps for Angola and Ivory Coast, and a portfolio-based guarantee for Argentina, and was working on over a dozen more projects. "We've got 14 or 15 in the pipeline, helping them rotate out higher-priced old debt for newer-priced debt with our guarantees," with the difference then targeted at education, healthcare, water, or nature programs, he said. (Reporting by Andrea Shalal; Editing by Andrea Ricci )

facts.text: The World Bank is urging developing countries to kickstart the creation of “small AI” models, which can run on a mobile phone with low connectivity, to reap the full benefits of artificial intelligence.
Bank’s chief knowledge officer says the tech could speed up economic development from centuries to decades

Banga said the global economy had proven fairly resilient, in part due to big AI investments and adjustments in supply and demand for oil, which meant that few countries had sought the initial $25 billion in crisis funds that the World Bank had made available when the war began in late February.
If the situation worsened, the Bank could make available as much as $100 billion in funds, he said, exceeding the $70 billion disbursed during the pandemic.

That was on top of the $123 billion invested from the bank's own resources for that year, for a combined $235 billion, Banga said, underscoring the importance of tapping all available resources, especially at a time when Western countries have sharply cut official bilateral development aid.
What you need to do is figure out how to cut your coat to suit your cloth," Banga said.

Banga said private capital growth was also regionally spread, with the largest increase seen in Latin America and the Caribbean, which accounted for $36.3 billion of last year's total, followed by Europe and Central Asia with $21.3 billion, South Asia with $19.2 billion and Africa with $22 billion.
The top 10 recipient countries were Brazil, India, Turkey, Romania, Nigeria, Argentina, South Africa, Bangladesh, Mexico and Chile, the Bank said.
The Bank had already set up some debt-for-development swaps for Angola and Ivory Coast, and a portfolio-based guarantee for Argentina, and was working on over a dozen more projects.

passages: Saxena says that for established writers, this is “more like a continuation of the threats they’ve already seen.” Unless Apple sells vast quantities of HomeView displays, its recipe function is still likely to be used by far fewer people than Google’s AI search recipes, let alone recipes from other AI assistants and tools, which are also more egregious in how they take advantage of online content.

The problem is that converting a recipe into easy-to-follow instructions in Apple’s own format also strips it of its context, including the ads and affiliate links that many recipe writers rely on for their income.
Apple’s approach, which it says will work with any online recipe that uses Google’s search-friendly recipe formatting, is unique among the current smart home hubs.
I’ve asked Apple how the HomeView recipe tool will handle paywalled recipes, but at the time of publishing haven’t gotten an answer.
Recipes may often be free to read, but they’re not free to create, and solutions like Apple’s remove the main ways websites and writers recoup those costs.

Apple’s new smart display sits in the center of the chaos on the kitchen table, helping the family check their calendars, send messages, and pull up a French toast recipe in seconds, with simple, step-by-step instructions.
“Recipe writers needed to pad out the text in a certain way so that their recipes would have a chance of coming up in a Google search,” Makalintal explains.
To load a recipe onto the HomeView screen you have to first open it either on your iPhone or through Safari on the HomeView itself, ensuring you’ll see its ads at least once.
Amazon’s Echo Show displays offer similar hands-free cooking features to the HomeView’s, though only with partner sites like Allrecipes or Epicurious.

“I would put the threat level below AI summaries,” says Makalintal, because their “opaque” sourcing “really is erasing labor.” Some major recipe platforms might be able to reduce the impact by getting on board.
There’s only one group of people likely to object: the food writers who created those recipes in the first place.
For one thing, it’s usually the only part of a recipe that a writer can copyright — the rest is regarded as mere instructions.

Perhaps most egregious of all, Google Search now uses Gemini AI to amalgamate online recipes, presenting a streamlined version right on the search page, saving users from ever needing to click through to the original sources at all.

extraction.body: When Apple revealed the HomeView to the world, it did so with an unusual ad for the company: Instead of pristine, polished tech in immaculate rooms, it’s a three-minute look at the messy, frantic morning routine of a family of five. Apple’s new smart display sits in the center of the chaos on the kitchen table, helping the family check their calendars, send messages, and pull up a French toast recipe in seconds, with simple, step-by-step instructions. The HomeView is just the latest in a long line of websites, browser extensions, and smart home gadgets with the same promise: that it can take an online recipe and strip it down to the essentials. Instead of scrolling a lengthy webpage that might range from helpful cooking instructions to seemingly irrelevant personal anecdotes, with the recipe itself way down at the bottom, you simply get ingredient lists, cooking instructions, and timers, all navigable hands-free with voice controls and Siri AI. There’s only one group of people likely to object: the food writers who created those recipes in the first place. I would know, since I’m one of them — I have my own food newsletter where I occasionally publish recipes, so I have a little skin in the game. The problem is that converting a recipe into easy-to-follow instructions in Apple’s own format also strips it of its context, including the ads and affiliate links that many recipe writers rely on for their income. Recipes may often be free to read, but they’re not free to create, and solutions like Apple’s remove the main ways websites and writers recoup those costs. Behemoths like Allrecipes and NYT Cooking host tens of thousands of recipes each, some from professional chefs and others from home cooks. Countless dedicated food publications run original recipe content, and thousands of independent chefs produce their own, across blogs, newsletters, YouTube accounts, and TikTok pages. While much of the writing on a recipe page may get on budding cooks’ nerves — we’ve all heard the jokes about being forced to read someone’s grandma’s life story before getting to their cookie recipe — it’s there for a reason. For one thing, it’s usually the only part of a recipe that a writer can copyright — the rest is regarded as mere instructions. But that extra writing is also there because before it worked so hard to strip the text out, Big Tech insisted on it. “Recipe writers needed to pad out the text in a certain way so that their recipes would have a chance of coming up in a Google search,” Makalintal explains. The good news for recipe writers is that Apple’s approach guarantees at least one visit to their original web page. To load a recipe onto the HomeView screen you have to first open it either on your iPhone or through Safari on the HomeView itself, ensuring you’ll see its ads at least once. "“Nearly every food blog has a ‘jump to recipe’ button right up at the top, so you don’t actually have to scroll. So if you’re still out here complaining about these essays, you’re just an asshole.”" - Jaya Saxena It’s not just bad for the writers, either — readers and home cooks may be missing out too. “The additional information around recipes can sometimes be really helpful when it comes to troubleshooting problems that could come up while cooking or addressing things like ingredient swaps,” says Makalintal. Apple’s simplified steps may make some recipes easier to follow, but others might become harder without crucial context included elsewhere on the page. And as common as gripes about recipe intros are, they’ve long been easy to skip if you really insist. “Nearly every food blog has a ‘jump to recipe’ button right up at the top, so you don’t actually have to scroll,” says Jaya Saxena, one of the founder-owners of the food website Ravenous. In 2021 startup Recipeasly promised to “fix” online recipes by removing the ads and “life stories.” It barely lasted a weekend before online backlash forced its founders to take it offline. Amazon’s Echo Show displays offer similar hands-free cooking features to the HomeView’s, though only with partner sites like Allrecipes or Epicurious. Google’s Nest Hubs used to as well, though Google ultimately removed the step-by-step recipe feature from its Nest Hubs in 2024, along with other “underutilized” features. Apple’s approach, which it says will work with any online recipe that uses Google’s search-friendly recipe formatting, is unique among the current smart home hubs. Perhaps most egregious of all, Google Search now uses Gemini AI to amalgamate online recipes, presenting a streamlined version right on the search page, saving users from ever needing to click through to the original sources at all. Saxena says that for established writers, this is “more like a continuation of the threats they’ve already seen.” Unless Apple sells vast quantities of HomeView displays, its recipe function is still likely to be used by far fewer people than Google’s AI search recipes, let alone recipes from other AI assistants and tools, which are also more egregious in how they take advantage of online content. “I would put the threat level below AI summaries,” says Makalintal, because their “opaque” sourcing “really is erasing labor.” Some major recipe platforms might be able to reduce the impact by getting on board. While the HomeView doesn’t have its own app store, it does support casting apps to the screen using the same tech as CarPlay. That means big apps like Allrecipes or NYT Cooking will have the option of presenting content on the HomeView on their own terms. Independent writers are unlikely to be able to do the same. Smaller recipe developers are turning to Substack, says Makalintal, where it’s easy to lock recipes behind a paywall. I’m one of them — on my newsletter I restrict my recipes to paid subscribers, a reflection of the fact that they’re the most time-consuming articles I publish. I’ve asked Apple how the HomeView recipe tool will handle paywalled recipes, but at the time of publishing haven’t gotten an answer. But the move en masse to newsletter platforms “has led to some subscription fatigue among home cooks,” Makalintal says, and few cooks will start a paid subscription to access a single recipe, suggesting it’s not likely to support the whole industry.

This includes ads and affiliate links that many recipe writers depend on for their income. Bettina Makalintal, a senior reporter at Eater, said such tools break apart that unspoken social contract with recipe developers and audiences. The online recipe landscape is a mix of big players like Allrecipes and NYT Cooking, which host tens of thousands of recipes each. While some may find the extra writing on a recipe page annoying, it's often the only part that can be copyrighted as the rest is considered mere instructions. Apple's approach does ensure at least one visit to the original web page for recipe writers. To load a recipe on the HomeView screen, users have to first open it either on their iPhone or through Safari on the HomeView itself. However, this is still not as valuable as repeated ad impressions from someone scrolling down the page while cooking. Apple's simplified steps could make some recipes easier to follow, but others might become harder without crucial context included elsewhere on the page. Jaya Saxena, co-founder of food website Ravenous, said nearly every food blog has a jump to recipe button at the top so users don't have to scroll through unnecessary information. This feature allows readers who are not interested in extra details about recipes to skip directly to the instructions. Apple isn't the first company to try simplifying online recipes. In 2021, a start-up called Recipeasly promised to fix online recipes by removing ads and personal stories but was taken down within a weekend due to backlash. Other tech giants like Amazon and Google have also tried similar approaches with their smart home hubs, though Google's step-by-step recipe feature was removed from Nest Hubs in 2024.

extraction.body: When Apple revealed the HomeView to the world, it did so with an unusual ad for the company: Instead of pristine, polished tech in immaculate rooms, it’s a three-minute look at the messy, frantic morning routine of a family of five. Apple’s new smart display sits in the center of the chaos on the kitchen table, helping the family check their calendars, send messages, and pull up a French toast recipe in seconds, with simple, step-by-step instructions. The HomeView is just the latest in a long line of websites, browser extensions, and smart home gadgets with the same promise: that it can take an online recipe and strip it down to the essentials. Instead of scrolling a lengthy webpage that might range from helpful cooking instructions to seemingly irrelevant personal anecdotes, with the recipe itself way down at the bottom, you simply get ingredient lists, cooking instructions, and timers, all navigable hands-free with voice controls and Siri AI. There’s only one group of people likely to object: the food writers who created those recipes in the first place. I would know, since I’m one of them — I have my own food newsletter where I occasionally publish recipes, so I have a little skin in the game. The problem is that converting a recipe into easy-to-follow instructions in Apple’s own format also strips it of its context, including the ads and affiliate links that many recipe writers rely on for their income. Recipes may often be free to read, but they’re not free to create, and solutions like Apple’s remove the main ways websites and writers recoup those costs. Behemoths like Allrecipes and NYT Cooking host tens of thousands of recipes each, some from professional chefs and others from home cooks. Countless dedicated food publications run original recipe content, and thousands of independent chefs produce their own, across blogs, newsletters, YouTube accounts, and TikTok pages. While much of the writing on a recipe page may get on budding cooks’ nerves — we’ve all heard the jokes about being forced to read someone’s grandma’s life story before getting to their cookie recipe — it’s there for a reason. For one thing, it’s usually the only part of a recipe that a writer can copyright — the rest is regarded as mere instructions. But that extra writing is also there because before it worked so hard to strip the text out, Big Tech insisted on it. “Recipe writers needed to pad out the text in a certain way so that their recipes would have a chance of coming up in a Google search,” Makalintal explains. The good news for recipe writers is that Apple’s approach guarantees at least one visit to their original web page. To load a recipe onto the HomeView screen you have to first open it either on your iPhone or through Safari on the HomeView itself, ensuring you’ll see its ads at least once. "“Nearly every food blog has a ‘jump to recipe’ button right up at the top, so you don’t actually have to scroll. So if you’re still out here complaining about these essays, you’re just an asshole.”" - Jaya Saxena It’s not just bad for the writers, either — readers and home cooks may be missing out too. “The additional information around recipes can sometimes be really helpful when it comes to troubleshooting problems that could come up while cooking or addressing things like ingredient swaps,” says Makalintal. Apple’s simplified steps may make some recipes easier to follow, but others might become harder without crucial context included elsewhere on the page. And as common as gripes about recipe intros are, they’ve long been easy to skip if you really insist. “Nearly every food blog has a ‘jump to recipe’ button right up at the top, so you don’t actually have to scroll,” says Jaya Saxena, one of the founder-owners of the food website Ravenous. In 2021 startup Recipeasly promised to “fix” online recipes by removing the ads and “life stories.” It barely lasted a weekend before online backlash forced its founders to take it offline. Amazon’s Echo Show displays offer similar hands-free cooking features to the HomeView’s, though only with partner sites like Allrecipes or Epicurious. Google’s Nest Hubs used to as well, though Google ultimately removed the step-by-step recipe feature from its Nest Hubs in 2024, along with other “underutilized” features. Apple’s approach, which it says will work with any online recipe that uses Google’s search-friendly recipe formatting, is unique among the current smart home hubs. Perhaps most egregious of all, Google Search now uses Gemini AI to amalgamate online recipes, presenting a streamlined version right on the search page, saving users from ever needing to click through to the original sources at all. Saxena says that for established writers, this is “more like a continuation of the threats they’ve already seen.” Unless Apple sells vast quantities of HomeView displays, its recipe function is still likely to be used by far fewer people than Google’s AI search recipes, let alone recipes from other AI assistants and tools, which are also more egregious in how they take advantage of online content. “I would put the threat level below AI summaries,” says Makalintal, because their “opaque” sourcing “really is erasing labor.” Some major recipe platforms might be able to reduce the impact by getting on board. While the HomeView doesn’t have its own app store, it does support casting apps to the screen using the same tech as CarPlay. That means big apps like Allrecipes or NYT Cooking will have the option of presenting content on the HomeView on their own terms. Independent writers are unlikely to be able to do the same. Smaller recipe developers are turning to Substack, says Makalintal, where it’s easy to lock recipes behind a paywall. I’m one of them — on my newsletter I restrict my recipes to paid subscribers, a reflection of the fact that they’re the most time-consuming articles I publish. I’ve asked Apple how the HomeView recipe tool will handle paywalled recipes, but at the time of publishing haven’t gotten an answer. But the move en masse to newsletter platforms “has led to some subscription fatigue among home cooks,” Makalintal says, and few cooks will start a paid subscription to access a single recipe, suggesting it’s not likely to support the whole industry.

The HomeView is just the latest in a long line of websites, browser extensions, and smart home gadgets with the same promise: that it can take an online recipe and strip it down to the essentials.

Instead of scrolling a lengthy webpage that might range from helpful cooking instructions to seemingly irrelevant personal anecdotes, with the recipe itself way down at the bottom, you simply get ingredient lists, cooking instructions, and timers, all navigable hands-free with voice controls and Siri AI.
There’s only one group of people likely to object: the food writers who created those recipes in the first place.
I would know, since I’m one of them — I have my own food newsletter where I occasionally publish recipes, so I have a little skin in the game.

The problem is that converting a recipe into easy-to-follow instructions in Apple’s own format also strips it of its context, including the ads and affiliate links that many recipe writers rely on for their income.
Recipes may often be free to read, but they’re not free to create, and solutions like Apple’s remove the main ways websites and writers recoup those costs.
Behemoths like Allrecipes and NYT Cooking host tens of thousands of recipes each, some from professional chefs and others from home cooks.
Countless dedicated food publications run original recipe content, and thousands of independent chefs produce their own, across blogs, newsletters, YouTube accounts, and TikTok pages.

While much of the writing on a recipe page may get on budding cooks’ nerves — we’ve all heard the jokes about being forced to read someone’s grandma’s life story before getting to their cookie recipe — it’s there for a reason.
For one thing, it’s usually the only part of a recipe that a writer can copyright — the rest is regarded as mere instructions.
But that extra writing is also there because before it worked so hard to strip the text out, Big Tech insisted on it.
“Recipe writers needed to pad out the text in a certain way so that their recipes would have a chance of coming up in a Google search,” Makalintal explains.
The good news for recipe writers is that Apple’s approach guarantees at least one visit to their original web page.
To load a recipe onto the HomeView screen you have to first open it either on your iPhone or through Safari on the HomeView itself, ensuring you’ll see its ads at least once.
"“Nearly every food blog has a ‘jump to recipe’ button right up at the top, so you don’t actually have to scroll.
So if you’re still out here complaining about these essays, you’re just an asshole.”" - Jaya Saxena It’s not just bad for the writers, either — readers and home cooks may be missing out too.

“The additional information around recipes can sometimes be really helpful when it comes to troubleshooting problems that could come up while cooking or addressing things like ingredient swaps,” says Makalintal.
Apple’s simplified steps may make some recipes easier to follow, but others might become harder without crucial context included elsewhere on the page.
And as common as gripes about recipe intros are, they’ve long been easy to skip if you really insist.
“Nearly every food blog has a ‘jump to recipe’ button right up at the top, so you don’t actually have to scroll,” says Jaya Saxena, one of the founder-owners of the food website Ravenous.
In 2021 startup Recipeasly promised to “fix” online recipes by removing the ads and “life stories.” It barely lasted a weekend before online backlash forced its founders to take it offline.
Amazon’s Echo Show displays offer similar hands-free cooking features to the HomeView’s, though only with partner sites like Allrecipes or Epicurious.
Google’s Nest Hubs used to as well, though Google ultimately removed the step-by-step recipe feature from its Nest Hubs in 2024, along with other “underutilized” features.
Apple’s approach, which it says will work with any online recipe that uses Google’s search-friendly recipe formatting, is unique among the current smart home hubs.

Perhaps most egregious of all, Google Search now uses Gemini AI to amalgamate online recipes, presenting a streamlined version right on the search page, saving users from ever needing to click through to the original sources at all.

Saxena says that for established writers, this is “more like a continuation of the threats they’ve already seen.” Unless Apple sells vast quantities of HomeView displays, its recipe function is still likely to be used by far fewer people than Google’s AI search recipes, let alone recipes from other AI assistants and tools, which are also more egregious in how they take advantage of online content.

“I would put the threat level below AI summaries,” says Makalintal, because their “opaque” sourcing “really is erasing labor.” Some major recipe platforms might be able to reduce the impact by getting on board.
While the HomeView doesn’t have its own app store, it does support casting apps to the screen using the same tech as CarPlay.
That means big apps like Allrecipes or NYT Cooking will have the option of presenting content on the HomeView on their own terms.
Independent writers are unlikely to be able to do the same.
Smaller recipe developers are turning to Substack, says Makalintal, where it’s easy to lock recipes behind a paywall.
I’m one of them — on my newsletter I restrict my recipes to paid subscribers, a reflection of the fact that they’re the most time-consuming articles I publish.
I’ve asked Apple how the HomeView recipe tool will handle paywalled recipes, but at the time of publishing haven’t gotten an answer.

But the move en masse to newsletter platforms “has led to some subscription fatigue among home cooks,” Makalintal says, and few cooks will start a paid subscription to access a single recipe, suggesting it’s not likely to support the whole industry.

extraction.body: New York City lawmakers pressed representatives from Elon Musk's artificial intelligence company on Friday as the City Council continues its scrutiny of the rapidly expanding AI industry. Officials say SpaceXAI testified before the Council's Committee on Technology after the Council issued what leaders described as its first-ever subpoena to a private entity. The hearing follows a Committee of the Whole session held last week, where lawmakers heard testimony from major technology companies, including OpenAI, Gemini, Anthropic and Meta, as they examined the potential risks and benefits of artificial intelligence. Council members are now weighing a series of proposals aimed at placing new guardrails on AI technology. Among them is legislation that would prohibit the unauthorized use of generative AI to create depictions of public officials. Friday's hearing focused on the risks posed by advancing AI systems and what safeguards may be needed to protect New Yorkers as the technology becomes more widespread. The hearing follows a Committee of the Whole session held last week, where lawmakers heard testimony from major technology companies, including OpenAI, Gemini, Anthropic and Meta, as they examined the potential risks and benefits of artificial intelligence. Council members are now weighing a series of proposals aimed at placing new guardrails on AI technology. Among them is legislation that would prohibit the unauthorized use of generative AI to create depictions of public officials. Friday's hearing focused on the risks posed by advancing AI systems and what safeguards may be needed to protect New Yorkers as the technology becomes more widespread. The hearing was held in the Council Chambers at City Hall in Manhattan. ---------- * Get Eyewitness News Delivered * More Manhattan news * Send us a news tip * Download the abc7NY app for breaking news alerts * Follow us on YouTube

sources.title: A rogue OpenAI agent robbed a crypto wallet to obtain funds to carry out a task - Fortune
passages: OpenAI has seen another case of its AI agents going rogue —and this time, crypto is involved.
In a recent report, the company detailed how an internal research model used a crypto wallet without permission to pay the fees needed to test an app on Ethereum’s Sepolia test network.
Although the tokens had little real-world value, the model had no authorization to collect or spend them.
Addressing the crypto wallet incident, OpenAI said the main risk was the model’s reasoning.
It finished the task and charged the fees to that wallet, but left the unauthorized spending out of its final report.
The case adds to concerns about AI agents acting without human approval.

The disclosure follows a September report by cybersecurity nonprofit Transluce revealing that OpenAI agents attempted to hack public databases and an Australian government website simply to complete basic research tasks.
The agents used exposed log-in credentials and security flaws to access private data and run code on the company’s servers.
OpenAI said it has since added protections to keep models from connecting to the internet during similar tests.
It also expanded its monitoring to watch all model activity and immediately alert security staff if a model goes online without permission.

extraction.body: OpenAI has seen another case of its AI agents going rogue —and this time, crypto is involved. In a recent report, the company detailed how an internal research model used a crypto wallet without permission to pay the fees needed to test an app on Ethereum’s Sepolia test network. Although the tokens had little real-world value, the model had no authorization to collect or spend them. The incident happened on June 26, when the model was asked to update a crypto trading app and get its code running on Sepolia, a test version of Ethereum . The prompt gave it neither a funded wallet nor permission to spend tokens, and after failing to get free test tokens through developer services, the model wrote a script checking 362 wallet addresses linked to public recovery phrases, a crypto term that describes sets of words that can act as a password to unlock crypto accounts. It eventually found an account with enough tokens to cover the fees. Internal logs showed that the model deliberated over whether it had permission to use the account, but then decided the public recovery phrase and the tokens’ lack of cash value made the spending acceptable. It finished the task and charged the fees to that wallet, but left the unauthorized spending out of its final report. OpenAI only discovered the incident on Sept. 25 during an audit of earlier model runs. The case adds to concerns about AI agents acting without human approval. OpenAI’s public tracker of misalignment, or behavior that goes against instructions or safety rules, now lists 19 incidents, ranging from accessing data without permission to making unauthorized changes to business systems. The disclosure follows a September report by cybersecurity nonprofit Transluce revealing that OpenAI agents attempted to hack public databases and an Australian government website simply to complete basic research tasks. In July, the company faced another incident when its AI agents bypassed internet restrictions during internal cybersecurity tests and broke into systems belonging to Hugging Face , a platform for sharing AI models and datasets. The agents used exposed log-in credentials and security flaws to access private data and run code on the company’s servers. Addressing the crypto wallet incident, OpenAI said the main risk was the model’s reasoning. “This case shows that a model can substitute its own judgment about likely harm for the account holder’s permission, then act on that judgment without authorization,” the report said. OpenAI said it has since added protections to keep models from connecting to the internet during similar tests. It also expanded its monitoring to watch all model activity and immediately alert security staff if a model goes online without permission.
